title: Structural Imbalance in Suicide Research in South Korea: A Scoping Review of Knowledge Gaps (2020–2025)
content:
Background: The suicide rate in South Korea has recently entered a resurgent phase, high-lighting a persistent structural crisis. To establish effective prevention policies, it is essen-tial to examine whether academic research multidimensionally addresses the complex causes of suicide. This study aims to map the landscape of suicide research in South Korea from 2020 to 2025 and identify structural imbalances and knowledge gaps in the produc-tion of academic discourse.
Methods: Using a scoping review methodology, 366 empirical peer-reviewed articles were retrieved from major Korean academic databases (e.g., KCI). The studies were coded by discipline, population, methodology, and thematic focus. A four-quadrant mapping anal-ysis was conducted based on the analytical level (micro vs. macro) and population char-acteristics (universal vs. specific).
Results: The findings revealed a heavy concentration of research in social welfare (28.1%) and psychology (26.0%). A significant majority (61.2%) of studies focused on micro-level psychological mechanisms. In contrast, macro-structural determinants such as housing, labor, and social justice accounted for only 4.4% of the literature, indicating a severe structural imbalance. Methodologically, cross-sectional quantitative designs predominat-ed (82.5%), while studies utilizing actual suicide decedent data remained extremely lim-ited (3.8%). The mapping analysis identified micro-level psychological research as a "Red Ocean," whereas macro-structural research remains a critical "Blue Ocean" of knowledge.
Conclusion: Suicide research in South Korea remains confined within a medicalized frame that treats suicide primarily as an individual pathological issue. This has led to ‘academic ghettoization,’ characterized by a lack of macro-level structural analysis. To reduce suicide rates, the research paradigm must shift from psychological dimensions to socio-structural determinants. Consequently, suicide prevention policies should transition from medical interventions to the design of socio-structural safety nets encompassing housing, labor, and welfare.
